<explanation>
The project is a Python library and set of applications built around a multi-agent architecture that streamlines common data science tasks. Its purpose is to provide an “AI Data Science Team” where each agent specializes in activities such as data cleaning, wrangling, feature engineering, SQL queries, exploratory data analysis, machine learning (via H2O and MLflow), and even multi-agent coordination (for combined tasks like data analysis with visualization).

Below are detailed instructions on how to create an accurate and detailed system design diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Core Library (“ai_data_science_team”): This is the heart of the project. It houses:
     - The Agents submodule (found under ai_data_science_team/agents) that contains individual agents for data cleaning, loading, visualization, wrangling, feature engineering, and SQL operations.
     - The Data Science Agents (ds_agents) responsible for exploratory data analysis (EDA) and related functions.
     - Machine Learning Agents (ml_agents) which include agents interfacing with H2O and MLflow for ML model building and deployment.
     - Multi-Agents (multiagents) that combine functionalities (for example, a Pandas data analyst that integrates data wrangling with visualization or SQL analysis).
   • Supporting Modules:
     - Tools (data loaders, EDA utilities, SQL connectors, etc. in ai_data_science_team/tools).
     - Templates and Parsers that assist in code generation and configuration.
     - Utilities (like logging, plotting, HTML helpers, regex, etc.) under ai_data_science_team/utils.
     - Orchestration (ai_data_science_team/orchestration.py) which likely coordinates and manages flows between agents.
   • Applications Folder (apps): Contains concrete AI-powered data science apps based on the core library – for instance:
     - Exploratory Data Copilot
     - Pandas Data Analyst App
     - SQL Database Agent App

2. Define the Relationships and Interactions:
   • The central orchestration module manages the calling of various agents. This module acts as the “director” that invokes proper agents based on user instructions.
   • Each agent in the Agents, ds_agents, ml_agents, and multiagents directories is specialized for a distinct task. They often communicate with supporting tools (found in the tools and utils directories), which in turn abstract lower-level functionality (for example, data formatting, plotting, and SQL connections).
   • The apps layer interacts with the core library via a well-defined API, using the agents to perform end-to-end workflows (e.g., load data → clean data → engineer features → run models).
   • External files (such as CSV, Excel files, databases, etc.) are inputs passed into the processing chain managed by the agents.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • Modular design: The code is organized into clear modules based on functionality, promoting separation of concerns.
   • Agent-based architecture: Different agents accomplish focused data science tasks. This design is extensible (with additional agents such as the future “Supervisor” or “Interpretability Agent”).
   • Integration and orchestration: The orchestration script ties individual components together in a pipeline style.
   • Technology stack includes Python with support for machine learning libraries (H2O, MLflow), data visualization (Plotly, Matplotlib), and data manipulation (pandas).

4. Guidelines for Drawing the Diagram:
   • Create a high-level diagram that visually divides the system into several major sections:
     - Core Library Components:
       ▪ Agents: Data Agents (data cleaning, loading, wrangling, visualization); Data Science Agents; ML Agents; Multi-Agents.
       ▪ Supporting Modules: Tools, Parsers, Templates, Utils.
       ▪ Orchestration Module: The central controller.
     - Applications Layer: Use cases wrapped as standalone apps that interface with the core library.
     - Data Sources: Illustrate external data files (CSV, Excel, database connections) fed into the system.
   • Use directional arrows to indicate data flow. For example:
     ▪ Arrows from “Data Sources” → “Applications” → “Orchestration Module” → “Agents” → “Tools/Utils” → back to the Applications for user output.
   • Differentiate components using shapes or colors:
     ▪ Rectangles might represent modules.
     ▪ Hexagons (or another distinct shape) for agent types.
     ▪ Cloud symbols to represent external data or services.
   • Label each component clearly. For instance, add labels like “Data Cleaning Agent”, “Feature Engineering Agent”, “H2O ML Agent”, etc.
   • Include annotations to highlight interactions and dependencies (e.g., “uses”, “invokes”, “processes”).

5. Tailor the Diagram to This Project’s Purpose:
   • Since this is a full-stack tool for AI-powered data science, stress the modular separation between core libraries (focused on backend processing) and the applications layer that interfaces with the end user.
   • Emphasize the agent-based approach: show how the different specialized agents work both independently and collaboratively within a coordinated pipeline.
   • Demonstrate how the core components (agents, orchestration, and supporting modules) integrate with external data through the apps.

6. Essential Diagram Elements for the Principal Software Engineer:
   • Include clearly labeled modules for “Agents”, “Orchestration”, “Tools/Utils”, “Templates/Parsers”, and “Applications”.
   • Use directional arrows to represent data flow from external data sources (CSV, Excel, SQL databases) through the orchestration and then into agent processes, with any intermediary tool usage.
   • Apply color coding or shape differentiation: for instance, use one color for agent modules, another for supporting libraries, and another for apps.
   • Provide annotations or brief descriptions near each component to explain its role.

Following these detailed steps will help ensure that the system design diagram captures all the essential architectural components of the AI Data Science Team project and clearly demonstrates how they interact to deliver high-performance data science tasks.
</explanation>
